The 2026 United States Senate elections were held on November 3, 2026, with 33 of the 100 seats in the Senate being contested in regular elections. In these elections, voters elected candidates to six-year terms that begin on January 3, 2027, and expire on January 3, 2033. The Senate Democratic Caucus is projected to have gained a majority, winning at least 54 seats, which would be their largest majority after an election since 2012.
Senators are divided into three classes whose terms are staggered, so that a different class is elected every two years. Class 2 senators were last elected in 2020. With the election of John Thune as leader of the Republican Conference, this was the first election year since 2006 in which Senate Republicans were not led by Mitch McConnell. The Senate Democratic Conference has been led by Chuck Schumer since 2017.
Special elections were also held in Ohio and Florida, following the resignation of JD Vance to become vice president and Marco Rubio's resignation to become United States secretary of state. The appointed incumbents in these races were Republicans Jon Husted and Ashley Moody, both of whom were running in their special elections to complete their terms until 2028.
Two incumbent senators—Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and John Cornyn of Texas—lost renomination in their respective primaries, while two nominees—Graham Platner (who dropped out) and Lindsey Graham (who died)—were replaced by a convention in Maine and a special primary in South Carolina, respectively. In three states (Idaho, Nebraska, and South Dakota), the Democratic nominee withdrew from the race, effectively clearing the field for an independent candidate.
Democrats have won 20 out of 35 contested seats, including 7 Republican-held seats. Republicans have successfully defended 13 seats, and two seats (Alaska and Mississippi) remain undecided as of November 6, 2026, 1 PM EST.
